paras: The lynching of Will Harris was the hanging of a Black prisoner by a mob of about fifty men who took him from officers aboard a Yazoo and Mississippi Valley train at Black Bayou, near Glendora, Mississippi, in late July 1905. Harris was accused, with his brother, of shooting two white men near Sharkey, and white newspapers from Mississippi to Wisconsin carried the hanging as a short news item. A Greenwood dispatch singled out one detail: members of the mob handed the deputy sheriff back his handcuffs and told him they were no longer needed.

According to a Mississippi paragraph printed in the Macon Beacon and the Leader, Harris was "one of the two brothers" who shot Messrs. Barksdale and Allen on the T. G. James place near Sharkey on July 19. Other papers stated the charge differently: the Starkville News said he was "charged with implication in the shooting of two white men," the Manning Times said he was lynched "for killing a white man," and the Lexington Dispatch said he "had seriously wounded a white man." A digest item went further, stating that "Harris and his brother killed two men." The Mississippi paragraph itself did not say whether Barksdale and Allen survived.

Harris was in the custody of officers, among them Deputy Sheriff Taylor of Greenwood, who were carrying him by train past Glendora. At Black Bayou a mob of "over fifty men" boarded the train and took him away from the officers. The men carried him about a quarter of a mile from the railroad and hanged him from the limb of a tree. The Mississippi account said the hanging was done quietly and that the mob then dispersed without disorder.
Late that afternoon, as Taylor was returning to Greenwood, members of the mob met him, gave him the handcuffs in which Harris had been held, and told him they were no longer needed.

The Greenwood dispatch described the returned handcuffs as "the official notification" that Harris "had paid the penalty for shooting a white man in Mississippi." No report of an inquest, arrests, grand jury action or trial appears in the coverage, and none of the reports says what became of Harris's brother.

Every report of the lynching appeared in a white newspaper, and no Black-press account appears in the coverage. The first items, on August 2, were brief: the Manning Times in South Carolina ran two lines under "Lynched by a Mob," while the Miller Sun in South Dakota printed a special from Glendora headed "Negro Murderer Hanged to a Tree." On August 3 the Goldsboro Weekly Argus in North Carolina carried the Greenwood dispatch under "Got the Handcuffs Back," calling the mob's gesture "as grim as it was novel."

Mississippi papers supplied the most detail. The Starkville News placed the lynching among its general news items on August 4, and on August 5 the Macon Beacon and the Leader printed an identical paragraph that named Barksdale and Allen and stressed that the mob acted "quietly" and left "without any disorder." The story then circulated in weekly digests, appearing in the Lexington Dispatch on August 9 and, with Harris described as "a negro murderer," in the Hocking Sentinel of Ohio on August 17 and the Wausau Pilot of Wisconsin on August 22. Across these versions the papers called Harris a "negro" and a "murderer," treated the accusation against him as established, and printed no criticism of the mob.

The date of the lynching is uncertain in the coverage. The Greenwood dispatch, dated July 29, said Taylor lost his prisoner "yesterday," which would place the lynching on July 28. The Glendora special and the Lexington Dispatch said only that it happened on "Tuesday," and the Starkville News ran the item among news of July 23 to 26, which also points to a date in late July. Accounts also differed on the charge, ranging from wounding one white man to killing two men, and on the place, which most gave as Black Bayou while one digest put the mob "at Glendora."
